title: The toll at the gate

data.source: Wald (1944), Wald (1945), Doob (1953), Siegmund (1979); cited from memory. Simulated sampled walks, seeded.

prediction: The mean number of steps to a cut and the mean surplus are Wald's identities: E[sum] = E[step] E[N] and E[B] = E[N] E[backward step], each within 1 per cent; the arithmetic S = 2B/sigma holds on every occasion, while Wald gives only the average; and a cut is one edge of Wald's two-edged test, so most walks with reversed drift never cut.
baseline: Wald's identities (1944) and sequential test (1945); Doob's optional stopping theorem (1953). Decoy: the same formula with no overshoot term.
relation: identical in the mean; R3 itself needs no theorem; the cut is one half of the sequential test
status_line: CRR here is: a special case of Wald's identities (the mean wait and the mean surplus); the arithmetic S = 2B/sigma needs no theorem, and the cut is one edge of Wald's two-edged test.
why: The mean wait and the mean surplus of a sampled half-turn are Wald's first identity applied to the steps and to their backward parts, to the tolerances written down. R3 (Phoenix status RESULT) is arithmetic true of each path; Wald adds the average size, which R1 to R6 do not state. The spread of the surplus is not given by either. The wider notes' M18 (their tier T1, conjecture) calls the cut an optimal stopping time; the optimality theorem is about a strip with two edges and R2 (ASSUMPTION) has one, so with the drift reversed most walks never cut.
